steps.title: Origin with rules
steps.body: France created the Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, AOC, in 1935, after decades of fraud and phylloxera. Today it's called AOP in EU terms, though AOC is still used. Each appellation defines the area, grapes, yields, minimum alcohol and some winemaking. INAO, the national institute, manages them.

steps.title: Nesting
steps.body: Appellations nest from broad to precise. In Burgundy: the regional Bourgogne, then village names like Gevrey-Chambertin, then Premier Cru and Grand Cru vineyards. The smaller the area, the stricter the rules and the higher the expected quality. Below AOP sits IGP, like Pays d'Oc, with looser rules; below that, Vin de France.

steps.prompt: Order these Burgundy levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each step narrows the area and tightens the rules.

steps.title: What it controls
steps.body: Appellation rules can set maximum yields, minimum ripeness, permitted grapes, planting density and even pruning. They don't usually require grapes to be named on the label, which is why French labels rarely mention them. The idea is that place, not grape, defines the wine.
steps.highlight: Rules on grapes, yields and methods

steps.prompt: Why do most French labels not name the grape?
steps.explanation: The appellation's rules define the grapes, so the place name tells informed drinkers what's in the bottle.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The AOC system, since 1935, ties wine to place with rules
Appellations nest from region to village to vineyard
Rules cover grapes, yields and methods; labels lead with place
